cordial

/KOR-juhl/ - the stress falls on KOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Cordial means warm, friendly, and heartfelt in a courteous way — real warmth carried by good manners.

Their rivalry on the tennis tour is famous, but at the net the two champions are unfailingly cordial — warm words, real smiles, and a handshake that lingers.

Example

When the visiting team's bus broke down in a snowstorm, the home coach's welcome was cordial in the fullest sense: hot soup in the cafeteria, a warm gym to stretch in, and a handshake for every player who would be trying to beat his squad the next evening.

The warmth is real — soup, shelter, handshakes — and it flows through simple courtesies toward people he has every competitive reason to keep at arm's length. That heartfelt friendliness, delivered politely and without gush, is what cordial describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

genial: Genial is sunny good cheer that belongs to a person's own temperament — a genial man beams at everyone. Cordial names the warmth shown between people, and it can hold even where the two have every reason to be cold.

gracious: Gracious is courtesy with generosity in it, flowing naturally from a host or from whoever holds the higher position. Cordial is that same warmth exchanged on equal footing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

frosty: coldly unfriendly in manner

hostile: openly unfriendly, treating someone as an enemy

Where it sits · how far the courtesy warms past mere form

polite → cordial → effusive

polite vs. cordial: Polite is weaker than cordial: politeness follows the forms correctly and can stay stone cold, while cordial manners carry real warmth from the heart.

effusive vs. cordial: Effusive is stronger than cordial: cordial warmth stays measured and courteous, while effusive greetings gush and overflow past anything the occasion asked for.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cord-: heart (Latin cor, cordis)

Suffix — -ial: relating to, characteristic of

Put it together: Cord- (Latin cor, cordis, 'heart') + -ial = of the heart. Medieval physicians prescribed cordials — drinks believed to strengthen the heart — and the adjective keeps the anatomy: cordial warmth is friendliness that comes from the heart, not just from the etiquette book.

Use the root in a new word: concord: The town's two rival bakeries have settled into a wary concord, each keeping to its own side of the square.

Root Check

Word Choice

warm / formal

Cordial does a job its neighbors in this unit can't: affable and amiable describe a person's easy friendliness, and amicable describes dealings free of conflict, but cordial names warmth delivered through courtesy — and it shines brightest between people who owe each other nothing more than politeness. That's why diplomats keep 'cordial relations,' and why a cordial handshake between rivals means something. You may also meet the noun: a cordial was once a drink to strengthen the heart.
